title: Three ways AI compute is being paid for
dek: Banks, a private equity firm and the stock market are each financing the AI buildout in a different way.

body.head: Banks finance the chips
body.text: A $63 billion transaction to enable the deployment of AI compute capacity for Anthropic will be executed through a newly formed special purpose vehicle. Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first lien portion, with Blackstone as the sole provider of the committed portion of the second lien financing.
support: Bank of America (NYSE: BAC ), Blackstone (NYSE: BX ), Citi (NYSE: C ) and Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS ) (the "Lead Financial Partners") today announced a $63 billion transaction to enable the deployment of AI compute capacity, leveraging Broadcom Inc.'s (NASDAQ: AVGO ) technology, for Anthropic.

The transaction will be executed through a newly formed special purpose vehicle ("SPV") with committed financing from the Lead Financial Partners to support the purchase of Broadcom XPU AI accelerators and networking solutions to be leased to Anthropic.
The first lien portion of the financing is being arranged by Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley, with Blackstone as the sole provider of the committed portion of the second lien financing.

body.head: Private equity buys and leases
body.text: SpaceX disclosed a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management buying the hardware and leasing it to SpaceX.
support: SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday .
Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX.

body.head: Meta turns to shareholders
body.text: Meta plans to sell new stock to raise money for its AI infrastructure buildout, and The Information reports the total could reach $95 billion. The Class C shares are described as carrying no voting rights, which lets Meta raise money without diluting Zuckerberg's control.
support: Meta plans to sell new stock to raise money for its AI infrastructure buildout.
According to The Information, the company plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares .
The Class C shares, which Meta announced last week, carry no voting rights.
That lets Meta raise money without diluting Zuckerberg's control.

body.head: What we can watch
body.text: Put side by side, these three stories show lenders, private equity and shareholders each carrying part of the cost of AI infrastructure. For those of us in credit and risk, a fair question is where our own institutions sit in these structures, and whether we can see who is on the other side of the lease.
